title: Untouched by pain and pleasure
hook: the one untouched by pleasure, pain, greed, attachment and pride is the Lord's image (Salok M9, ang 1427)

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghatt: the Lord lives in every heart. Today's salok says what it looks like when that light shines through.

Someone stands at the bakery counter at the end of a long day. The smell hits. The craving arrives like a wave: just one, you deserve it, it's been a terrible afternoon. They stand there. And sometimes, if they simply wait, something surprising happens. The wave crests, and then it falls. Thirty seconds later, the want is smaller. Two minutes later, it's gone. From the inside, a craving can feel permanent. This one wasn't. The thirteenth salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur describes a person these waves can't knock over, and then gives that person a startling name.
screen: `THE BAKERY COUNTER.` → `A CRAVING, LIKE A WAVE.` → `IT CRESTS, THEN FALLS.`

segments.voice: The salok says, in paraphrase: the one whom pleasure and pain don't touch, nor greed, attachment or pride: says Nanak, listen, O mind, that one is the very image of God. The key verb is parsai, to touch, to brush against. These waves come to everyone. The salok doesn't say this person never meets pleasure or pain, greed or pride. They come and don't stick, like rain running down a window while the glass stays clear. Then the startling name: moorat bhagvaan, the image of God. Moorat means a form, an image, the word used for statues in temples. Sikhs don't worship images. And yet here, in the last pages of the Granth, the ninth Guru uses that very word for a living person: not stone, but a human being whose heart isn't pushed around. The Mool Mantar, the opening of the Granth, calls God akaal moorat, the form beyond time. The same word. There it describes the Timeless; here, a person clear enough to show it. And it builds on yesterday. The salok before this one said the Lord lives in every heart. In this picture, the waves of craving and pride cover that light, the way waves cover the sand. When they settle, it shows. So becoming untouched isn't about becoming hard. It's about becoming clear, so the One already inside can be seen.
screen: `PARSAI: THE WAVES DON'T STICK.` · `MOORAT BHAGVAAN: GOD'S IMAGE.` · `AKAAL MOORAT, THE SAME WORD.` · `CLEAR ENOUGH TO SHOW THE LIGHT.` · then, large: `UNTOUCHED.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe, and wait for any want to arise, to check your phone, to snack, to move; when it comes, don't act and don't fight, just watch it like a wave, rising, cresting, beginning to fall, and count the breaths it takes. You're practicing being touched without being moved. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths.
Moorat, a form, an image. The thirteenth salok calls the one whom pleasure, pain, greed, attachment and pride don't touch moorat bhagvaan, the very image of God.
Your line: untouched. Not hard, just clear enough for the light to show. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok among the ninth Guru's saloks at the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and often cite it to say that a person free of craving and pride shows the image of God.

chat.says: Sikhs don't worship images, so why does a salok call a person God's image?
options: Because someone untouched by craving and pride is clear enough to show God's light.
It means holy people should be worshipped instead of statues, as living idols.
It means anyone who never feels pleasure or pain at all has actually become God.
